source_text: Denique sine cunctatione tribuens quae poposci, quidque ex his confectum esset aspiciens, profiteris te ad hoc quod exstruximus, imbecillum esse; apostolum Paulum illis omnibus quae diximus, obviare; quem tamen inducis eadem quae tu dederas, concedentem. Ais enim: Apostolus neque voluntatem arguit parvuli, quae propria in illo nondum est ad peccandum [n42] ; quo dato iam convictum est, nec posse in illo quodpiam esse peccatum, cuius nulla alia conditio est, secundum definitionem quoque tuam, quam voluntas admittendi quod iustitia vetat, et unde liberum est abstinere.
pass_a_gloss: Finally, granting without delay the things I asked, and looking at what had been brought about from these, you profess that you are weak toward this which we have built; that the apostle Paul opposes all those things which we have said; whom nevertheless you bring in as granting the same things which you had given. For you say: The Apostle accuses neither the will of the little child, which as his own is not yet in him toward sinning; by which given it has already been convicted that neither can there be any sin in him whose no other condition is, according to your definition also, than a will of admitting what justice forbids, and from which it is free to abstain.

lemmas.lexica: LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will
LS liber=free; Blaise unde liberum est abstinere
LS parvulus; Blaise infants in original-sin debate

pass_b_english: In fact, you grant what I asked without hesitation. Seeing what follows from these concessions, you acknowledge that you are powerless against the case we have built. You say the apostle Paul opposes everything we have said, yet introduce him as conceding the same points you had conceded. For you say: ‘The apostle does not accuse the infant’s will, which does not yet exist in the infant as a personal will capable of sin’ (Augustine, Marriage and Desire 2.45). Once this is granted, it is already proved that there cannot be any sin in the infant. For sin, even according to your own definition, has no other nature than the will to commit what justice forbids and from which one is free to abstain.

choices.why: Julian's forensic/moral fault tied to will, not a substance in nature.
Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
